newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British Land beats profit forecasts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British Land beats profit forecasts.

text.p: British property group British Land reported a 47 percent increase in annual pre-tax profits to 91.2 million pounds ($149.3 million) on Wednesday, far exceeding analysts' expectations.
Profits for the year ending March 31 were up from 62.1 million pounds for the same period a year before. Analysts polled by Reuters last week forecast a range of 75 to 79 million pounds.
"Improvements in the economy coupled with low rates of interest and inflation have created a more favourable climate for property," British Land's chairman John Ritblat said in a statement.
Analysts said the results were encouraging but some warned that there was unlikely to be much more upside for the share price.
"The profit figures were excellent," said Nan Rogers, analyst at Charterhouse Tilney. "We will be increasing our profit forecast for next year."
The shares were 1-1/2p higher at 589 in the morning session.

The group's net assets rose 14.3 percent to 487 pence per share and while on a fully-diluted basis the growth was 12.7 percent to 478 pence from 424 pence, British Land has since issued a convertible bond which would lift the figure to 493 pence per share.

British Land now has total funds under management, including partners' shares of joint ventures, of 5.8 billion pounds. Its total property portfolio, including its share of joint ventures, has reached 5.1 billion pounds.

The group, which has concentrated its business in Britain and Ireland, said its revenues were mainly from net rents, which had risen 28 percent to 260.4 million pounds a year, while gross rents rose 25 percent to 299.8 million pounds.
"For a fourth successive year the net rate of gain is greater than the gross, showing that we continue to achieve higher rental productivity," Ritblat said.
Property trading made profits of 7.1 million pounds, up from 1.1 million, marking the 21st successive year British Land had made profits from this area at an average six million a year.

John Weston Smith, the group's finance director, told Reuters British Land would be looking at further joint ventures following the success of recent property link-ups with Scottish and Newcastle Plc, Great Universal Stores and Tesco.
"I think there will be more (joint ventures), quite where and when I can't say but they are something we look to do," Weston Smith said.
British Land likes to establish joint ventures with non-property groups, provides the property expertise, splits the venture 50/50 and raise separate finance.

This means it does not use up its own credit, expands assets under management on which it can get growth, widens its spread and reduces risk and gives it management fees. "They (joint ventures) have got a lot of merits," Weston Smith said.
The firm's London Corn Exchange development had been nearly completely let and what was not yet let was almost all under offer, but Weston Smith declined to disclose the rent level.
He said British Land expected to develop further vacant sites on Euston Road in central London but while he would not rule out a speculative development he said this was less likely.
And the firm is waiting for a response to its application for planning permission for the redevelopment of the Plantation House site in the City of London.
British Land was recently named in a report as a possible bidder for rival MEPC but Weston Smith said such rumours were commonplace.

While there were possible mergers in the sector, such moves were always difficult not only because of the complications involved in such deals but also when share prices were at a premium as they currently are, he added.
But British Land was not likely to embark on the acquisition trail.

"We've been interested in share stakes from time to time, but corporate activity is pretty difficult to do unless you can get a very strong position. I dont see it as a line we are going to go along."
($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
